answers.question_text: With reference to a THREE phase electrical distribution system: (a) explain the advantages and disadvantages of an insulated neutral system; (8) (b) state how an earthed neutral system is earthed and the measures taken to limit the maximum earth fault current. (2)
answers.answer_text:
(a) Insulated (unearthed) neutral system

In an insulated neutral system, the star point of the generator or transformer has no deliberate low-impedance connection to earth - the only path to earth is through the system's natural, distributed capacitance to the hull, a very high impedance path.

Advantages:
1. Continuity of supply on a single fault - since there's no deliberate low-impedance earth path, a single phase-to-earth fault doesn't create a large fault current and doesn't force an automatic trip. Propulsion, steering, and essential services can keep running with a fault present somewhere in the system.
2. Limited fault energy on the first fault - only a small capacitive charging current can flow (typically low single-digit amps on a ship's LV system), minimal risk of arc damage or fire from that first fault.
3. Time to act safely - the vessel can complete a critical manoeuvre or reach a safe location while the fault is traced and isolated methodically.

Disadvantages:
1. Voltage rise on healthy phases - the moment one phase earths, its voltage to earth collapses toward zero, but the two healthy phases rise to full line voltage relative to earth - an increase of √3 (approximately 1.73x) above normal. This sustained overvoltage continuously stresses the healthy phases' insulation for as long as the fault remains uncleared.
2. Risk of a cross-country (double) fault - if a second earth fault develops on a different phase before the first is cleared, the result is effectively a phase-to-phase short circuit through the hull.
3. Fault location takes time and system knowledge - because nothing trips automatically, engineers typically isolate sections one at a time while watching the insulation monitoring device.
4. Total reliance on the monitoring device working - the entire safety benefit depends on the insulation monitoring device being installed, functioning, and its alarm being noticed and acted on.
5. Transient overvoltages from arcing faults - an intermittent, restriking earth fault can produce voltage spikes considerably higher than the steady-state √3 rise.

(b) Earthed neutral system

The star point is connected to the ship's hull through a Neutral Earthing Resistor (NER), rather than solidly earthed. The NER is sized to limit maximum earth fault current to a controlled, low value - enough to reliably operate an earth-fault relay/alarm, but low enough to avoid the arc damage and fire risk that an uncontrolled high fault current would cause.
answers.examiner_focus: The genuine marker's report for this July 2017 sitting notes most candidates handled this well, but a number lost marks by conflating two distinct fault types: an earth fault (a phase conductor making unintended contact with earth/the hull) versus single phasing (loss of one phase entirely, typically due to an open circuit, with no phase-to-earth contact involved). Worth stating explicitly which one you mean.

answers.question_text: (a) Explain, with the aid of a sketch, the principle of operation of an earth leakage detection system of the instrument type. (6) (b) Explain why an insulated neutral system is used extensively on board ships. (2) (c) State, with reasons, why a single earth fault on an insulated neutral system should always be cleared as soon as possible. (2)
answers.answer_text:
(a) Instrument-type earth leakage detection system

This system uses a sensitive centre-zero moving-coil milliammeter, connected across the system so that it continuously measures any current leaking from the phase conductors to earth through the ship's insulation resistance. Typically the meter is connected between the neutral/star point and earth (or via a network of equal high-value resistors from each phase to a common point, with the meter reading the resulting current at that point). Under healthy conditions, insulation resistance is high, so only a very small, steady leakage current flows and the meter reads near zero. If insulation deteriorates anywhere on the system, or an actual earth fault develops, the leakage current increases measurably, the meter deflects, and this triggers a visual/audible alarm.

Worth explicitly distinguishing this from the simpler earth lamp indicator method: three lamps, each connected from one phase to earth. Under healthy conditions all three glow at similar brightness. If one phase develops an earth fault, that lamp dims or goes out while the other two brighten. The earth lamp method gives only a rough visual indication; the instrument type gives an actual measured value on a meter.

(b) Why insulated neutral systems are used extensively at sea

A single earth fault does not immediately create a large fault current or force a shutdown, since there's no solid earth return path. Propulsion and essential services can continue running even with a fault present, critical at sea where an unplanned blackout is far more dangerous than a monitored, uncleared fault.

(c) Why a single earth fault must still be cleared promptly

The two healthy phases rise to full line voltage relative to earth (approximately 1.73x) for as long as the fault remains, stressing their insulation. If a second earth fault develops on a different phase before the first is cleared, the result is effectively a phase-to-phase short circuit - far more severe than either fault alone.
answers.examiner_focus: Across three verified sittings (Oct 2020, Dec 2021, Oct 2022), examiners repeatedly flagged the same specific error: candidates sketching and describing earth lamps when the question specifically asked for the instrument type. One report noted this question would likely be reused and hoped the message about this exact confusion would get through by then. Read exactly which variant of a system is named, don't default to the simpler/more familiar version.
answers.sketch_description: Schematic: three phase lines (R, Y, B) at top, each connected through an equal high-value resistor (zigzag symbol) down to a common junction point. From that common point, a line down to a centre-zero milliammeter, then down to an earth/hull symbol (ground hatching). A separate small side panel contrasts this with the earth lamp method (three lamps, phase to earth, visual only).

answers.question_text: (a) Explain the principle of operation of an insulation resistance test, stating why the test is carried out on a regular basis. (6) (b) Describe how EACH of the following electrical tests is carried out: (i) resistance; (2) (ii) continuity. (2)
answers.answer_text:
(a) Insulation resistance (IR) test

A DC test voltage - commonly 500V for testing low-voltage equipment such as a 440V winding - is applied between the conductor under test and earth (or between separate windings), using an insulation resistance tester (Megger). The instrument measures the resulting leakage current and displays the insulation resistance in megohms. Sound insulation gives a high reading; the reading falls only if insulation has degraded through moisture ingress, contamination, or ageing. It's carried out on a regular basis because insulation deteriorates progressively - regular testing catches a downward trend early, before it develops into an earth fault or winding failure.

(b)(i) Resistance test

Measures the actual resistance of the conductor or winding itself - not its insulation - typically using a low-resistance ohmmeter or Kelvin bridge. For a three-phase machine, comparing all three phase windings checks they're balanced; an abnormally high reading on one phase points to a loose connection or partial winding fault.

(b)(ii) Continuity test

Simply confirms an unbroken electrical path exists, using a continuity tester or multimeter's buzzer setting - testing a fuse is the classic example: continuity means the fuse is intact, no continuity means it's blown.
answers.examiner_focus: Two verified, genuine patterns (March 2021 and July 2022). First, a number of candidates answer part (b) by simply repeating their part (a) answer instead of describing three genuinely distinct procedures. Second, when asked for the resistance test in (b)(i), many candidates describe an IR/Megger test instead - the two are different: one tests insulation to earth, the other tests the conductor's own resistance. A concrete detail worth remembering: roughly 500V test voltage into a 440V winding.

answers.question_text: With reference to insulation testing of electrical equipment: (a) state the reasons for insulation testing and why it is carried out on a regular basis; (2) (b) describe the procedure for taking a set of insulation readings on an electric motor in-situ, stating the minimum acceptable readings; (6) (c) explain the term Polarisation Index. (2)
answers.answer_text:
(a) Insulation deteriorates over time from heat, moisture, oil contamination and mechanical stress. Regular testing - PMS routine, before running standby equipment, after overhaul - catches this early, before it progresses to an earth fault, allowing corrective action before failure.

(b) Procedure: isolate and lock off the motor, confirm dead with an approved voltage indicator, disconnect electronic control gear sensitive to test voltage. Select the correct test voltage (typically 500V DC for a low-voltage motor). Connect one lead to earth (motor frame) and test each phase winding to earth in turn; also test winding-to-winding if required. Take each reading after a consistent time interval (commonly 1 minute), noting ambient temperature and humidity.

Minimum acceptable reading: a practical guide is roughly 1-10 MΩ for low-voltage machines - a healthy new winding reads far higher (often several hundred MΩ), so the absolute minimum matters less than a clear downward trend against previous readings.

(c) Polarisation Index: the ratio of the insulation resistance reading at 10 minutes to the reading at 1 minute, during one continuous test. Sound, dry insulation shows resistance rising over that period as absorption currents decay, giving a PI ratio above 1 (commonly 2 or more is good). Poor/damp insulation shows little rise, giving a PI close to 1. PI reflects insulation condition independent of ambient temperature/humidity effects that distort a single-point reading.
answers.examiner_focus: Three verified diets. October 2021: candidates who said the test was to 'check the health of the machinery' or 'assess the condition' were marked down - answers must be specific: why does insulation resistance actually reduce, and what factors contribute? Part (c): most knew what PI was but few could give an actual numeric value - worth memorising the '2 or more is good' benchmark. Oct 2024 corroborates the same generic-answer trap. Reasonably well answered overall in October 2021, positive in Oct 2024/Mar 2026.

answers.question_text: (a) Sketch a circuit diagram of a self excited a.c. generator. (5) (b) Describe the operation of the circuit sketched in part (a). (5)
answers.answer_text: (a)/(b) Principle and operation: A self-excited generator supplies its own field excitation current from its own output, rather than needing a separate external DC supply or battery. The process relies on residual magnetism: a small amount of magnetism always remains in the rotor iron even when stationary. As the prime mover brings the rotor up to speed, this small residual field induces a small initial EMF in the stator windings. That small AC output is fed through a step-down transformer and rectifier bridge, producing a small DC current, delivered back to the rotor's field winding via slip rings - increasing the field strength slightly. This stronger field induces a larger stator EMF, which when rectified and fed back further increases field current again. This self-reinforcing build-up continues until the magnetic circuit begins to saturate, at which point output voltage stabilises at its rated value. No external battery or DC supply is ever needed - reliance on residual magnetism alone defines 'self-excited' as opposed to a separately-excited design.
answers.examiner_focus: Both verified sittings (March 2017, October 2022) show candidates generally understand the concept fine, but marks consistently separate on sketch completeness. March 2017's report notes fuller marks going to more complete, well-annotated sketches; October 2022 reports no problems. A fully labelled sketch - rectifier bridge, slip rings, feedback path back to the field winding, note on residual magnetism as the starting point - is what separates full marks from partial credit.

Rectifier output (DC) goes to a slip rings box. From slip rings, a feedback line back down and around to the generator's rotor field winding, closing the loop with an arrow showing 'field current increases rotor magnetism'.

answers.question_text: Describe, with the aid of a circuit diagram, the operation of an automatic voltage regulator (AVR) which employs the use of thyristors. (10)
answers.answer_text:
The AVR continuously compares the generator's actual output voltage - sensed via a voltage transformer/sensing circuit - against a fixed reference (set-point) voltage. Any difference is fed to a firing control circuit, which adjusts the point in each AC half-cycle at which the thyristors supplying the exciter/field winding are triggered (fired). Firing earlier in each half-cycle increases the average DC delivered to the field winding, increasing field current and generator output voltage; firing later reduces it. This forms a continuous closed loop - sense output voltage, compare to reference, adjust thyristor firing angle, adjust field current, adjust output voltage - correcting for load changes and keeping output voltage within a tight regulated band.

Expanded technical depth: Sensing stage - three-phase output stepped down via a voltage transformer, rectified to a DC signal proportional to true RMS voltage, sensing all three phases to detect unbalance too. Reference and comparison - sensed DC compared against a stable reference (Zener diode or IC internal reference) via an op-amp error detector, giving an error signal indicating direction and magnitude of correction needed. Firing/control stage - phase-angle control of the thyristors, giving fast response and no moving parts, which is why thyristor control replaced older carbon-pile/rotating-amplifier regulators. Field/exciter stage - controlled thyristor output supplies the exciter winding (brushless: feeds rotating exciter armature, rectified via rotating diode bridge to main rotor field; static/slip-ring: feeds main field directly via brushes). Protective functions commonly built in: volts-per-hertz (V/Hz) protection reducing the voltage reference if frequency falls, preventing core saturation/overheating; overexcitation limiting capping maximum field current; under-voltage protection signalling an alarm/trip if the AVR cannot maintain voltage despite full field current.
answers.examiner_focus: Verified feedback (December 2021, December 2024): 'most candidates that answered this question did well, scoring high marks and there were good sketches' / 'no real problems, been up plenty of times in the past.' A well-understood, positively received question across both sittings - a complete, correctly-labelled block diagram is what separates full marks from partial marks.
answers.sketch_description: Block diagram: Generator box -> Voltage sensing box -> Compare to reference box -> Firing circuit box -> feedback loop down and back to the generator via a thyristor bridge supplying the field winding. Closed loop clearly shown with arrows.

answers.question_text: (a) Describe, with the aid of a sketch, a static excitation system for a generator. (8) (b) Explain TWO advantages of static excitation. (2)
answers.answer_text:
(a) Unlike a brushless system (separate small rotating exciter generator with a rotating rectifier bridge), a static excitation system draws its excitation power directly from the main generator's own output terminals via a dedicated tapping or step-down transformer. This AC supply is fed through a controlled thyristor rectifier bridge, producing DC delivered to the main rotor field winding via slip rings and brushes. 'Static' refers to the excitation equipment itself (transformer, thyristor bridge) having no moving parts, unlike a rotating exciter armature - though slip rings and brushes remain necessary since excitation current still has to cross from stationary equipment to the rotating rotor.

(b) Two advantages: (1) Faster response - excitation power drawn directly from the generator's own terminals through solid-state thyristor control, with no separate rotating exciter's time-constant, responds very quickly to a voltage error signal, directly improving voltage-dip recovery speed. (2) Simpler and more reliable - no separate rotating exciter armature or rotating rectifier assembly to maintain, though slip rings/brushes still need periodic inspection and brush replacement.
answers.examiner_focus: July 2021's feedback was strongly positive - several candidates scored full marks with very good sketches. Worth noting the same diet's report on a related switchboard question criticised answers that left terms unqualified (e.g. 'voltage' without high/low, 'overheating' without explaining why) - reinforcing that every term and reason needs to be made specific.

answers.question_text: Describe, with the aid of a diagram, a shaft generator that uses a frequency converter.
answers.answer_text:
A shaft generator is driven directly (or via a step-up gearbox) by the ship's main propulsion shaft, generating electrical power as a byproduct of the main engine's rotation. Because the main engine runs at a speed dictated by propulsion requirements, not electrical requirements, the shaft generator's raw output frequency would vary directly with shaft speed - unacceptable for direct connection to the ship's electrical system, which needs a stable, fixed frequency.

A frequency converter solves this: the shaft generator's variable-frequency AC output is first fully rectified to DC via a rectifier bridge, completely removing the frequency variation by converting to a DC link. This DC is fed to an inverter (thyristors or IGBTs), which electronically synthesises a new, stable-frequency AC output matching the ship's standard busbar frequency, regardless of actual shaft speed or the generator's raw input frequency. This rectifier-DC link-inverter arrangement allows a shaft generator, despite running at whatever speed propulsion demands, to supply stable, standard-frequency power directly onto the ship's main switchboard, in parallel with the diesel generators if required.
answers.examiner_focus: No specific feedback located for the July 2016 occurrence. October 2022 reports simply 'no problems' - a straightforward, well-handled question there.
answers.sketch_description: Block diagram left to right: main propulsion shaft (thick line) into a 'Shaft generator' circle, output arrow to 'Rectifier (AC to DC)' box, arrow to 'Inverter (DC to AC)' box, arrow to 'Main switchboard' box. Label under the flow: 'Output frequency independent of shaft speed'.

answers.question_text: With reference to reverse power protection for a.c. generators operating in parallel: (a) explain why traditional reverse power relays, operating on mechanical principles, have been replaced by electronic digital microprocessor types; (2) (b) describe, with the aid of a sketch, a generator reverse power protection circuit that uses an electronic phase sensitive detector. (8)
answers.answer_text:
(a) Traditional mechanical relays (induction spinning-disc mechanism reacting to reversed power flow via electromagnetic torque) have moving parts subject to wear and friction, and need periodic mechanical calibration. Electronic digital/microprocessor types offer faster and more accurate detection - important since reverse power can mechanically damage the prime mover quickly - precisely adjustable trip settings, self-diagnostic capability, no moving parts to wear or stick, and digital event logging.

(b) Reverse power occurs when a generator, instead of supplying power to the busbar, begins absorbing it - its prime mover no longer providing enough torque to overcome the electrical load (mechanical fault, fuel failure, governor mis-setting while paralleled), so the machine effectively starts 'motoring,' being driven by the other generator(s) on the bus.

The protection circuit takes two signals: a voltage reference from a VT across the generator terminals, and a current signal from a CT in the generator's output. The phase-sensitive detector continuously compares the phase relationship between these two signals. In normal operation (exporting power), current sits in a normal phase relationship relative to voltage. When the generator begins absorbing power instead, current effectively reverses relative to the voltage reference - the phase angle shifts by approximately 180 degrees, since power flow itself has reversed.

When the detector senses this reverse-power phase relationship, it feeds a time-delay circuit - deliberately included so a brief transient swing during normal load changes doesn't cause a nuisance trip. Only if the reverse condition persists beyond this set delay (typically several seconds) does the relay operate, tripping the generator breaker before the reversed power flow can mechanically damage the prime mover.
answers.examiner_focus: Extremely direct signal from October 2023: the examiner states this was a genuinely new-style question, most candidates scored badly because they didn't understand how the phase-sensitive detector actually works, and several defaulted to sketching the old, now-obsolete spinning-disc mechanical relay - earning essentially nothing relevant. The report explicitly states the old mechanical sketch is no longer worth practising and this modern-content question will very likely reappear. October 2024 corroborates: 'Candidates are getting the hang of this now, although the sketching could be improved. As an examiner I will not be asking for the older spinning disc type.'

Both feed into a 'Phase sensitive detector - compares phase' box, which feeds a 'Time delay' box, which feeds down and back to the generator breaker with label 'Trip signal to generator breaker if reverse power persists'.

answers.question_text: Explain why it is necessary to provide reverse power protection for a.c. generators operating in parallel. (Note: exact original question wording for this specific occurrence did not extract cleanly from the source PDF - genuine marker feedback confirms the topic was tested, tied to a July 2018 sitting.)
answers.answer_text:
If a generator's prime mover loses the ability to supply sufficient driving torque - fuel failure, mechanical fault, governor problem, or operator error reducing fuel too far - the generator doesn't simply stop, because it remains electrically connected to the other generator(s) on the same busbar. Instead, it continues to be driven, but now by the electrical system rather than by its own prime mover: it runs effectively as a synchronous motor, drawing power from the bus to keep its own shaft turning.

This is hazardous for three reasons. First, the affected prime mover - being mechanically driven while receiving no fuel or steam - can suffer real damage: a diesel engine motoring without combustion can lose proper lubrication conditions and overheat certain components; a steam turbine motoring without steam flow can overheat its blading from windage losses. Second, the other generator(s) on the system are now carrying the extra burden of driving the motoring machine, reducing their remaining spare capacity. Third, with spare capacity reduced, any subsequent load change or emergency demand has far less margin before risking a complete blackout.

Reverse power protection exists specifically to detect this condition automatically and trip the affected generator's breaker before mechanical damage occurs or the situation compounds - precisely why it's a mandatory fitted protection wherever generators run in parallel.
answers.examiner_focus: Genuine feedback tied to July 2018: many candidates opened their answer with 'SOLAS requires reverse power protection' and simply stated it prevents motoring, without ever explaining how the reverse power condition actually arises. Citing the regulation isn't what earns marks - explaining the physical mechanism (prime mover failure leads to generator motoring leads to drawing power from the bus) is what's tested.

answers.question_text: With reference to the protective devices fitted to a main alternating current generator, explain EACH of the following: (a) overcurrent and short circuit protection; (2) (b) generator negative phase sequence; (2) (c) loss of field (excitation); (2) (d) undervoltage; (2) (e) reverse power. (2)
answers.answer_text:
(a) Overcurrent and short circuit protection: inverse-time overcurrent relays (or a generator breaker with adjustable overcurrent trip settings) monitor output current via CTs. If current exceeds a preset threshold for longer than a set time delay (allowing brief starting currents to pass), the relay trips the generator breaker.

(b) Generator negative phase sequence: detects an unbalanced condition across the three output phases - a 'negative sequence' current component arising from an unbalanced load, single-phasing fault on a connected motor, or asymmetric system fault. Negative sequence current sets up a magnetic field rotating opposite to the rotor's normal rotation, inducing double-frequency eddy currents in the rotor surface and causing rapid, severe localised overheating - a risk ordinary overcurrent protection wouldn't catch, since total current might not exceed a normal threshold while still being dangerously unbalanced.

(c) Loss of field (excitation): detects loss of DC field excitation (AVR/exciter fault, slip-ring/brush failure). Without excitation the generator can't maintain synchronism and draws reactive power from the busbar to sustain a residual field, destabilising the system.

(d) Undervoltage: trips or blocks closing if generator terminal voltage falls below a set threshold - sustained low voltage risks connected motors overheating, and guards against closing onto a bus under a fault condition already suppressing voltage.

(e) Reverse power: trips the generator if it begins absorbing power from the bus (motoring) rather than supplying it, protecting the prime mover from mechanical damage.
answers.examiner_focus: One of the most consistently mishandled questions across the whole dataset, with the same two errors recurring across both verified diets (December 2019, October 2020). First: the stem explicitly specifies 'a main alternating current generator,' yet candidates gave generic textbook descriptions of overcurrent protection ('protects cables and conductors') without tailoring to a generator context - naming the actual protective devices/settings is what's being asked, not repeating the question stem. Second, and more striking: 'negative phase sequence' was misidentified as something else entirely in BOTH diets - described as reverse power in one sitting, and as synchronising/paralleling in the other. Worth being precisely explicit that it means phase-current imbalance inducing a reverse-rotating magnetic field and rotor overheating, distinct from both.

answers.question_text: With reference to main a.c. generators: (a) state the immediate and subsequent actions to be taken in the event of a high windings temperature alarm being activated; (8) (b) state the feature of the windings cooler tubes that prevent damage to the windings in the event of leakage. (2)
answers.answer_text:
(a) Immediate action: reduce load on the affected generator as far as practicable - bringing another generator online in parallel to share load if not already running - to reduce heat being generated. Confirm cooling air or water flow is actually functioning (fans running, cooling water valves open, coolers not blocked). If temperature continues rising despite reduced load and confirmed cooling flow, prepare to remove the generator from service in a controlled manner - bring a standby unit online first, reduce the affected generator's load to zero, then open its breaker - rather than waiting for an automatic trip.

Subsequent action: once safely removed from service (or if temperature stabilises and it remains running), investigate the root cause - checking cooling air filters or water strainers for blockage, checking for excessive ambient temperature in the generator space, and checking for genuine electrical causes such as overload, unbalanced load/negative phase sequence, or a developing insulation fault. The generator shouldn't return to full service until the cause is identified and corrected.

(b) The windings cooler (an air-to-water heat exchanger cooling the generator's internal ventilating air) is arranged so the cooling water side operates at a lower pressure than the air side. If a cooler tube develops a leak, this pressure differential means water tends to leak outward into the air stream/drain rather than being drawn under pressure into the winding space - protecting the windings from water ingress and consequent electrical fault.
answers.examiner_focus: Verified in March 2025. No marker's report was available for this specific diet at time of writing.

Caption underneath: 'Subsequent: investigate root cause before returning generator to service.'

answers.question_text: With reference to the paralleling of a.c. generators: (a) outline the requirements of synchronisation; (2-3) (b) explain how KW power is shared; (1-2) (c) explain how Kvar power is shared; (1) (d) TWO VERIFIED VARIANTS: [variant 1] state SIX types of damage that may be caused when machines are incorrectly synchronised (6) OR [variant 2] list the features that the (Automatic) Power Management System controls for the operation of main switchboards and generators when the engine room is in unattended mode (4-5)
answers.answer_text:
(a) Requirements of synchronisation: before a generator can be safely closed onto a live busbar, four conditions must be matched between the incoming generator and the busbar: (1) Same voltage; (2) Same frequency; (3) Same phase sequence (R-Y-B order, checked at commissioning, doesn't change in normal operation); (4) Phase angle in coincidence - instantaneous voltage waveforms in phase at the moment the breaker closes. Checked using a synchroscope: a rotating-pointer instrument whose speed/direction shows fast/slow relative to the busbar, and whose position shows instantaneous phase difference. The breaker is closed when the pointer is at (or just approaching) 12 o'clock, rotating slowly in the fast direction - closing slightly before exact coincidence compensates for the breaker's own closing delay.

(b) How KW power is shared: controlled by adjusting the governor setting (speed droop) of each engine. Increasing fuel/steam admission to one prime mover increases that generator's share of total KW load without affecting frequency, since the other generator's governor compensates.

(c) How Kvar power is shared: controlled by adjusting each generator's field excitation (via its AVR). Increasing field current on one generator increases the reactive power it supplies without significantly affecting shared bus voltage.

(d) Variant 1 - damage from incorrect synchronising: closing a generator onto the busbar out of synchronism can cause: deformation of the alternator's stator end-windings from electromagnetic shock force; crack propagation in the coupling, shaft, or crankshaft from sudden torque reversal; twisting/shearing of the prime mover's flexible coupling; damage to circuit breaker contacts from very high fault-like current at closure; bearing damage from sudden mechanical shock loading; loosening of foundation bolts/mountings from transient vibration.

(d) Variant 2 - PMS features in unattended mode: automatic starting and stopping of standby generators based on load demand; automatic synchronising and load sharing when bringing a new generator online; automatic load shedding of non-essential consumers on approaching overload; preferential tripping sequences protecting essential services first; monitoring/alarm functions reporting generator status to the bridge/control room during unattended periods.
answers.examiner_focus: December 2018: candidates lose marks in part (d)-variant-1 by naming WHERE damage occurs (stator, rotor, crankshaft) rather than WHAT KIND of damage results (deformation, crack propagation, twisting). July 2022: several candidates answered part (a) with bare phrases like 'same frequency' or 'correct voltage' without stating these must match BETWEEN the incoming generator and busbar specifically - a few words don't earn full marks on a 3-mark part. July 2024: on part (d)-variant-1 again, some candidates said overcurrent/overload/reverse power/undervoltage - that's an answer for a DIFFERENT question (protective devices, not damage types); others stated 'damaged this, damaged that' without specifics like twisted armature shafts or broken coupling bolts.

answers.question_text: Describe, with the aid of a block diagram, the operation of a load sensing electronic governor controller for an a.c. generator. (10)
answers.answer_text:
A load-sensing electronic governor continuously monitors the generator's electrical output load (via CTs on the output, combined with voltage sensing to calculate actual KW) rather than relying solely on sensing a change in engine/shaft speed after the fact. Because electrical load changes at the busbar happen essentially instantaneously, sensing load directly - rather than waiting for the resulting speed droop to be detected mechanically - allows the governor to begin adjusting fuel/steam admission before a significant speed deviation has even had time to develop, giving a faster response than older speed-only governors.

Block diagram, described: Load sensing transducer (CTs/VTs on generator output, calculating actual KW) -> signal conditioning/comparator (comparing sensed load against the engine's current fuel setting) -> electronic control unit (computing required fuel rack/valve position to match the new load) -> actuator (electric or hydraulic actuator driving the fuel rack or steam governor valve) -> prime mover, with speed feedback (from a speed pickup on the shaft) closing an outer loop to fine-tune and correct for any remaining deviation, settling the engine precisely back to its set speed/frequency once the new load is matched.

This combination - fast-acting load anticipation plus a speed feedback trim loop - gives both quick initial response to a sudden load change and accurate final speed/frequency regulation.

July 2025 reports 'reasonably well answered although there were some very basic sketches' - a complete, properly-labelled block diagram (both the load-sensing path and the speed-feedback trim loop) is what separates full marks from a basic sketch.

A feedback line from the prime mover back up to the comparator labelled 'Speed feedback (trim loop)', closing an outer loop.

answers.question_text: Describe, with the aid of a block diagram, how automatic starting, load sharing and stopping of generators in response to load changes is effected. (10)
answers.answer_text:
Automatic starting: the Power Management System (PMS) continuously monitors total electrical load against available generating capacity. As load approaches a preset percentage of the running generator's capacity, the PMS automatically starts a standby generator, brings it up to speed, and - once at rated speed and voltage - automatically synchronises it (checking voltage, frequency, phase sequence, phase angle coincidence) before closing its breaker onto the live busbar.

Load sharing: once paralleled, KW load is shared by the PMS adjusting each engine's governor setting; Kvar (reactive) load is shared by adjusting each generator's AVR/field excitation - both automatically balanced so each generator carries a proportionate share of total load relative to its rating.

Automatic stopping: as total load falls, the PMS monitors the load that would remain if a generator were removed. Once remaining generators could safely carry the total load, the PMS unloads the generator due to be stopped (transferring its share to the others via governor/AVR adjustment), opens its breaker once its load has fallen to near zero, and allows it to run unloaded briefly for cooling before shutting down - avoiding an abrupt disconnection of a generator still carrying significant load.

Block diagram, described: Load sensing (CTs/VTs on the busbar) -> PMS logic comparing load against running capacity and preset thresholds -> start/stop signal to standby generator's automatic starting sequence -> synchronising check unit -> breaker close/open signal -> governor and AVR control for load/reactive sharing among all paralleled units.
answers.examiner_focus: July 2020's report notes this is a 'straightforward' question that 'has been up before' - a signal this is a recurring, well-established topic rather than one with a specific common trap. The value is in giving a complete, properly sequenced answer covering starting, synchronising, sharing, and stopping.
answers.sketch_description: Block diagram: 'Load sensing (busbar CTs/VTs)' -> 'PMS logic' box (comparing load vs capacity) -> branches to 'Start/stop signal' box -> 'Synchronising check unit' -> 'Breaker close/open' -> 'Governor + AVR control (sharing)' box, feeding back to the generators.

answers.question_text: With reference to automatic Power Management Systems for the control of the operation of main switchboards and generators: (a) list the features that the Power Management System controls in order to comply with the requirements for a vessel; (7) (b) explain how the generators and switchboard would be controlled following a failure of the Power Management System. (3)
answers.answer_text:
(a) Features the PMS controls: (1) Automatic starting of standby generators as load rises toward a preset percentage of running capacity. (2) Automatic synchronising and paralleling - bringing a starting generator up to speed and voltage, then closing its breaker onto the live busbar once synchronised. (3) Automatic load sharing - KW via governor adjustment, Kvar via AVR/excitation adjustment. (4) Automatic stopping of a generator once remaining load can be safely carried by fewer running units. (5) Load shedding/preferential tripping of non-essential consumers as load approaches or exceeds available capacity. (6) Blackout recovery - automatic restart and resynchronising sequence following a total loss of power. (7) Monitoring and alarm functions - continuously monitoring generator and switchboard parameters, reporting to the bridge or engine control room, specifically essential for UMS compliance.

(b) Following PMS failure: control reverts to fully manual operation - the duty engineer manually starts and stops generators based on observed load, manually operates the synchronising panel (checking the synchroscope, voltage, frequency) to parallel a generator, and manually adjusts governor and AVR settings to share load. Manual monitoring and manual shedding of non-essential consumers is required if approaching overload. Critically, continuous manned attendance in the engine room becomes necessary - the vessel cannot safely continue in unattended (UMS) mode without it.
answers.examiner_focus: Explicitly noted as the least popular electrical question in the July 2017 sitting, with vague responses to part (a); most candidates failed to give a genuinely full list of the automatic functions. The trap is answering with only two or three functions when seven marks require a comprehensive list - starting, synchronising, sharing, stopping, shedding, blackout recovery, and monitoring/alarms all need to appear.

answers.question_text: (a) Sketch a wiring diagram of a shore connection for the supply of electrical power to a vessel, showing the phase sequence indicator. (4) (b) TWO VERIFIED VARIANTS: [variant 1, Dec 2024] Explain the consequences of connecting an electrical shore supply in EACH of the following cases: (i) in the wrong phase sequence; (2) (ii) at a higher voltage; (2) (iii) at a higher frequency. (2) OR [variant 2, Jul 2026 - candidate's own sitting] Describe the procedure for shutting down running generators, stating precautions to be taken, prior to changing over to shore power. (6)
answers.answer_text:
(a) The shore power cable connects via a dedicated shore connection box through an isolating switch/breaker, with the three phases wired to the ship's main switchboard or a dedicated shore-supply busbar section. A phase sequence indicator is connected across the incoming shore supply specifically to confirm phase rotation matches what the ship's system expects, before the shore supply is actually connected. This is a fundamentally different check from paralleling two generators: since the ship's own generators are normally shut down when taking shore power, there's no dynamic voltage/frequency/phase-angle synchronising process at all - the phase sequence check is a static, pre-connection safety check.

(b) Variant 1 - consequences of incorrect connection:
(i) Wrong phase sequence: any three-phase motor would run in the wrong direction - reversing any two of three phases reverses the rotating field direction - risking serious damage to pumps, fans, or other rotating machinery running backwards.
(ii) Higher voltage: connected equipment (motors, transformers, lighting) would be over-voltaged, risking insulation breakdown and overheating.
(iii) Higher frequency: motors and frequency-dependent equipment would run faster than intended, with cooling fan performance also tied to frequency - risking overheating or mechanical overspeed damage if equipment isn't rated for the resulting altered speed and airflow.

(b) Variant 2 - shutdown procedure prior to shore changeover, both scenarios covered since the actual installation type varies:

Scenario 1 - Paralleled changeover (make before break): confirm shore power is correctly matched (voltage, frequency, phase sequence). Synchronise the shore supply onto the busbar exactly as paralleling a second generator - matching voltage, frequency, phase sequence, phase angle via the synchroscope. Gradually transfer load from the ship's generator onto shore power by reducing its governor setting toward zero output. Once carrying negligible load, open its breaker, then allow it to run unloaded briefly for cooling before shutting down the prime mover completely.

Scenario 2 - Break before make: used where switchgear isn't rated for paralleling with an unsynchronised external source. Shed or stand by non-essential loads first. Open the ship's generator breaker, briefly interrupting supply. Confirm shore power is correctly matched before closing the shore supply breaker to re-energise the busbar. Allow the disconnected generator to run unloaded briefly for cooling before shutting down.

Common to both: follow the vessel's own SMS/company procedure for exact sequencing, since this varies by installation. The underlying principle either way: never leave the busbar without a confirmed, correctly-matched supply at any point, and never shut down a generator carrying significant load without first transferring that load elsewhere.
answers.examiner_focus: December 2024: no candidate produced a sketch worth the full 4 marks in part (a) - this diagram clearly needs more deliberate practice. In part (b) variant 1, some candidates confused this scenario with generator reverse-power protection or with paralleling two live generators - worth being explicit that shore power connects to what is normally a dead, isolated ship's system, a different scenario entirely. Variant 2 (July 2026) verified only by the candidate's own attendance at that sitting - no marker's report published yet.
answers.sketch_description: Shore connection box on the left, wired through an isolating switch/breaker to the ship's main busbar on the right. A phase sequence indicator (small dial or three lamps) connected across the incoming shore-side phases, positioned before the isolating switch, clearly labelled 'checked before connection.'

answers.question_text: With reference to a.c switchboards: (a) state, with reasons, the protective devices that are fitted; (5) (b) state why a breaker may fail to open under prolonged low voltage conditions; (2) (c) explain the actions to be taken should a main generator circuit breaker stay connected despite repeated efforts to trip it off the board. (3)
answers.answer_text:
(a) Protective devices, with reasons: Overcurrent/short-circuit protection (breaker overcurrent trip or fuses) - protects cables and busbars from thermal/mechanical damage from fault or overload current. Undervoltage protection/release - trips or blocks closing if voltage falls too low, since low voltage risks motors overheating and prevents uncontrolled reclosure once voltage is restored. Reverse power protection (generator breakers) - trips if the generator absorbs power rather than supplying it, protecting the prime mover. Earth fault protection - detects and alarms/trips on a fault to earth. Preferential trip devices - disconnect non-essential loads in a pre-set sequence as the system approaches overload, protecting continuity of essential supply.

(b) Why a breaker may fail to open under prolonged low voltage: the breaker's trip coil/mechanism relies on a solenoid needing a minimum voltage/current to develop enough magnetic force to physically operate the tripping mechanism. Under prolonged low voltage, the trip coil may not receive sufficient current to generate enough force to release the latch, so the breaker can remain stuck closed despite a trip signal.

(c) Actions if a main generator breaker stays connected despite repeated tripping attempts: reduce the generator's load manually by adjusting the governor to cut fuel/steam admission, easing the immediate risk. If another generator is running in parallel, check the synchronising/load-sharing arrangement and manage load distribution manually. If the breaker genuinely cannot be opened electrically, prepare to shut down the affected generator's prime mover directly (fuel to zero) as a last resort. Isolate and investigate the breaker mechanically once safe, and report the fault for repair.
answers.examiner_focus: December 2016: several candidates stated protective devices in a handful of words (e.g. just 'undervoltage') without explaining the reason - a Chief's-level answer doesn't earn 5 marks for a list of names alone. August 2020: few candidates thought to mention checking the synchroscope as part of managing this scenario. March 2024 adds a critical safety point to part (c): under no circumstances should you trip a running engine directly if the breaker is stuck and won't trip on reverse power while still paralleled - do a controlled back-out or isolation of that switchboard section instead, safety first.

answers.question_text: With reference to the protection of electrical power circuits: (a) explain discrimination, describing how it is achieved. (5) (b) state, with reasons, the type of fuses used for protection; (3) (c) explain preferential tripping. (2)
answers.answer_text:
(a) Discrimination (selectivity): the principle that when a fault occurs anywhere in a distribution system, only the protective device closest to the fault should operate, isolating just the affected section while everything else remains in service. Achieved by grading the time delay and/or current setting of devices in series, so devices nearer the load operate faster (shorter delay, lower threshold) than devices further upstream. A fault on a small branch circuit trips its local device quickly; if that device fails, the next device upstream (deliberately set with a longer delay) operates as backup.

(b) HRC (High Rupturing Capacity) fuses are typically used for power circuit protection, since they can safely interrupt very high fault currents without violent rupture or dangerous arcing, and have well-defined, repeatable time/current characteristics important for reliable discrimination.

(c) Preferential tripping: an automatic, pre-arranged sequential load-shedding scheme that disconnects non-essential consumers in priority order as the system approaches overload capacity - deliberately sacrificing lower-priority loads to protect continuity of essential services rather than risk a complete blackout.
answers.examiner_focus: A specific, genuine confusion flagged in July 2019: some candidates described discrimination AS preferential tripping. They are genuinely different mechanisms - discrimination governs which protective device responds to an actual fault, isolating only the faulted section; preferential tripping deliberately sheds non-essential load as the system nears capacity, with no fault necessarily present at all.

answers.question_text: (a) With reference to the protection of electrical equipment in a distribution system: (i) state the aims of the protective devices; (3) (ii) list the parameters that are monitored and acted upon by the protective devices. (4) (b) State, with reasons, THREE causes of electrical fires. (3)
answers.answer_text:
(a)(i) Aims: detect an abnormal condition (overcurrent, short circuit, earth fault, overload) as quickly as possible, isolate only the affected part of the circuit before damage or fire can result, protect personnel from electric shock, and maintain continuity of supply to unaffected circuits.

(a)(ii) Parameters monitored: current (overcurrent/short-circuit detection), voltage (over/undervoltage), earth leakage current (earth fault detection), temperature (thermal overload, via a thermal element or embedded sensor), and time (the deliberate time-delay characteristic used to achieve discrimination).

(b) Three causes of electrical fires, with reasons: (1) Overloaded circuits - conductors carrying current beyond rated capacity generate excess heat that can ignite surrounding insulation. (2) Poor or loose connections - a loose terminal presents higher contact resistance, generating localised heating (and sometimes arcing) that can ignite insulation or debris. (3) Damaged or degraded insulation - aged, mechanically damaged, or oil-contaminated insulation can break down, allowing a short circuit or earth fault, with associated arcing and heat presenting a direct fire risk.
answers.examiner_focus: July 2021: several candidates gave answers that were too brief and left key terms unqualified, naming 'voltage,' 'temperature,' or 'frequency' as monitored parameters without stating whether the concerning condition is high or low; part (b) drew vague answers like simply 'overheating' without the actual underlying cause. Every parameter and reason needs to be made specific.

answers.question_text: With reference to overcurrent protection for electrical circuits: (a) explain THREE methods of protection, stating where EACH may be used; (6) (b) explain, with the aid of a diagram, the meaning of the term inverse current time characteristic. (4)
answers.answer_text:
(a) Three methods: (1) Fuses (typically HRC) - used on smaller, lower-cost circuits and as backup protection, replaced after operating. (2) MCB/MCCB - used on distribution circuits where resetting/reclosing after a transient fault without needing a replacement part is valuable. (3) Protective relays operating a circuit breaker - used on larger power circuits and generator/switchboard protection, where adjustable, selective tripping characteristics beyond a simple fuse or MCB are needed.

(b) Inverse current time characteristic: a protective device that operates faster the higher the fault current is, taking progressively longer to trip as current gets closer to its minimum pickup threshold. Shown as a graph of operating time (often logarithmic) against current (as a multiple of rated/pickup current): the curve falls steeply at first then flattens, so a small overload trips slowly (avoiding nuisance trips) while a severe fault trips almost instantly. This characteristic is specifically what allows discrimination between devices in series: a downstream device's curve is set to operate faster than the upstream device's curve for the same fault current.
answers.examiner_focus: October 2021: several answers were too brief for the six marks available on part (a), suggesting candidates named the three methods without giving enough explanation of where and why each is actually used.
answers.sketch_description: Graph: x-axis 'Current (multiple of rated)', y-axis 'Operating time (log scale)'. A curve starting high on the left (low current, long time) and falling steeply to a low, flat tail on the right (high current, near-instant trip). Two curves shown overlaid, one for a downstream device and one for an upstream device, with the downstream curve consistently below/faster, demonstrating discrimination.

answers.question_text: With reference to electrical shortcircuits: (a) state, with reasons, THREE factors that will influence the severity of a short circuit; (6) (b) explain the role of reactance when selecting protective devices. (4)
answers.answer_text:
(a) Three factors: (1) Distance from the source (generator/transformer) - a fault closer to the source sees less cumulative circuit impedance, so more current can flow, making it more severe than an equivalent fault further downstream. (2) System fault level (source impedance/generating capacity connected) - more generating capacity in parallel, or lower source impedance, delivers higher fault current for the same fault location. (3) Type of fault - a three-phase bolted fault is generally most severe (highest current), while a single-phase-to-earth fault on an insulated neutral system produces comparatively limited current.

(b) Reactance (particularly source and cabling inductive reactance) is a major component of total circuit impedance and directly limits maximum fault current at any given point. Protective devices must be selected with a fault-current rating (breaking capacity) at least equal to the maximum prospective fault current calculable at their installation point - calculated using total impedance, including reactance, between source and that point. A device with insufficient breaking capacity risks catastrophic failure rather than safely interrupting the fault.

answers.question_text: With reference to electrical system protective devices, explain the purpose of EACH of the following: (a) overcurrent protection; (2) (b) short circuit protection; (2) (c) no-volt protection; (2) (d) reverse power protection; (2) (e) preferential tripping. (2)
answers.answer_text:
(a) Overcurrent protection: protects conductors, cables and equipment from damage due to current in excess of rated capacity for a sustained period, disconnecting before resulting heat damages insulation or creates fire risk. Time-delayed, allowing brief harmless excursions.

(b) Short circuit protection: protects against a very high-magnitude fault current (direct phase-to-phase or phase-to-earth bolted fault), capable of severe near-instantaneous damage if not cleared immediately. Fast/instantaneous characteristic, little to no intentional delay.

(c) No-volt protection: prevents a machine or circuit from automatically restarting once voltage is restored after an interruption, without deliberate manual action - protecting personnel working on stopped equipment from an unexpected restart, and preventing an uncontrolled surge of multiple motors restarting simultaneously.

(d) Reverse power protection: trips the generator breaker if the machine begins absorbing power (motoring) rather than supplying it, protecting the prime mover.

(e) Preferential tripping: disconnects non-essential loads in a pre-arranged priority sequence as the system approaches overload, protecting continuity of essential supply.
answers.examiner_focus: July 2020: reasonably well answered, though some candidates stated rather than explained. December 2020: a lot of candidates couldn't clearly distinguish (a) from (b), giving vague/repetitive answers for both, and few gave concrete examples of the actual device providing each protection. On part (c), some candidates framed no-volt protection narrowly around preventing restart specifically after a blackout - a partial view; the fuller purpose covers any unannounced automatic restart on voltage restoration.

answers.question_text: (a) Sketch a circuit diagram of an emergency generator power supply and distribution system, indicating the essential services provided at 440 volts ac, 220 volts ac and 24 volts dc. (6) (b) State the regulations pertaining to the emergency generator. (4)
answers.answer_text:
(a) Emergency generator -> emergency switchboard -> distribution at 440V AC directly to larger essential loads (emergency fire pump, steering gear if required, emergency lighting distribution boards) -> a step-down transformer to 220V AC for smaller essential services (lighting circuits, communication equipment, some control systems) -> a transformer/rectifier arrangement providing 24V DC for battery charging and DC essential services (navigation lights, radio/GMDSS equipment, emergency alarm/communication systems) - typically including the emergency battery itself, kept on float charge and available even if the emergency generator hasn't started.

(b) SOLAS requires the emergency source of electrical power to automatically start and be capable of supplying essential services within 45 seconds of a main power failure, with sufficient capacity for a minimum specified duration (commonly 18 or 36 hours depending on vessel type). The emergency generator and switchboard must be located above the bulkhead deck, outside machinery spaces, in a readily accessible position, separated from the main machinery space by fire-resistant boundaries.
answers.examiner_focus: August 2020's feedback flagged one specific, concrete detail: several candidates omitted the rectifier needed to actually produce the 24V DC supply - the sketch must show the AC-to-DC conversion stage, not just a label. Also verified March 2025 and October 2025 (via candidate's own class attendance).

answers.question_text: (a) Sketch a circuit showing how the emergency generator is started, connected to the emergency busbars and how the main busbars are disconnected in the event of a blackout. (6) (b) Explain how an emergency generator can be tested to ensure that it is capable of satisfactorily delivering the rated power. (4)
answers.answer_text:
(a) On loss of main power, a voltage-sensing relay on the main busbar detects the failure and signals the emergency generator's automatic starting sequence (compressed-air or battery-electric start) to begin. Once the emergency generator reaches rated speed and voltage, an automatic changeover switch (interlocked so main and emergency supplies can never be connected together simultaneously) disconnects the emergency busbar from the dead main busbar connection and connects it instead to the emergency generator's output. The sketch needs to show: the voltage-sensing/starting-initiation relay, the starting arrangement, the emergency generator, and specifically the changeover switch mechanism between main and emergency supply - not the downstream distribution to individual services, which is a different question.

(b) Testing: run the emergency generator on load (using a dummy/test load bank, or transferring actual non-essential ship's load onto it) to confirm it can deliver full rated output without excessive voltage or frequency droop, checking automatic starting and changeover both function within the required time, run for a specified minimum duration to properly prove capability rather than just confirming the machine starts unloaded.

On part (b), few mentioned how long the generator would be run for or how load would be applied. December 2023's report is unusually detailed and effectively gives the model answer: three phases from the main busbars and three from the emergency busbars, with changeover switch, coil, and starting coil shown - the starting coil closes the battery circuit which energises the starter motor. This sketch is described as self-explanatory, which is why only a sketch (not written description) is asked for and awarded marks - text alone earned no credit in that sitting. Part (b) specifically means a proper load test, not starting the engine unloaded on a test switch. Also verified March 2026.

The emergency generator connects through an automatic changeover switch (shown as a two-position switch with mechanical interlock) to the emergency busbar, with the main busbar's connection point shown broken/disconnected at the same switch.

answers.question_text: (a) State FIVE essential electrical services that are able to be operable under fire conditions. (5) (b) Explain how electric cables for the essential services in part (a) pass through bulkheads whilst maintaining gas tight and water tight integrity. (3) (c) State the requirements for the cables which supply electrically driven emergency fire pumps. (2)
answers.answer_text:
(a) Emergency lighting, the emergency fire pump, fire detection and alarm systems, public address/general alarm systems, and steering gear (where electrically powered) - all needed to fight the fire, evacuate safely, and maintain vessel control while it's happening.

(b) Cables pass through purpose-built cable transits - typically a steel frame fitted into the bulkhead penetration, packed with a fire-resistant, water- and gas-tight sealing compound (or pre-formed sealing modules) around each individual cable, maintaining the structural fire rating and watertight integrity at the penetration point. Cable glands provide additional mechanical support and sealing where cables enter equipment or junction boxes.

(c) Cables must be fire-resistant type (rated to continue functioning for a specified period even when directly exposed to fire, not merely fire-retardant), and routed away from areas most likely to be affected by a fire - specifically avoiding the main machinery space, where a fire is statistically most likely to originate and where the pump is most needed to remain functional.

July 2024's report notes: candidates who produced a sketch for part (b) generally got full marks, and perhaps this should be asked for explicitly in future questions - worth including a simple sketch of the cable transit even though not strictly required by this wording.

answers.question_text: (a) Describe, with the aid of a block diagram, the operation of an a.c. input UPS arrangement. (7) (b) List SIX essential services that the UPS or emergency batteries may support. (3)
answers.answer_text:
(a) The AC mains supply is continuously rectified to DC, which simultaneously trickle-charges a standby battery bank and feeds a DC bus. This DC is continuously fed to an inverter, which converts it back to a stable AC output supplying connected essential loads - under normal conditions, power actually flows AC mains -> rectifier -> DC bus (battery on float charge) -> inverter -> AC output, rather than the load being connected directly to mains. If AC mains fails, the rectifier's DC output disappears, but the battery bank - already on the same DC bus - seamlessly continues supplying the inverter, which continues producing AC output with no interruption at all. This is what makes it genuinely 'uninterruptable,' unlike a standby generator which takes time to start - the battery bridges power until mains is restored or a backup generator takes over.

(b) Emergency lighting, navigation lights, radio/GMDSS communication equipment, fire detection and alarm systems, steering gear control circuits, and critical propulsion monitoring/alarm systems.

Arrow annotation showing the battery seamlessly bridges the DC bus if the rectifier's input fails.

answers.question_text: Describe the construction and operation of EACH of the following: (a) synchronous motor; (5) (b) induction motor. (5)
answers.answer_text:
(a) Synchronous motor: constructionally similar to an alternator run in reverse - a wound rotor (DC field excitation via slip rings, or increasingly a brushless static/rotating exciter) sits inside a three-phase stator winding. When the stator is energised, it produces a rotating magnetic field; the DC-excited rotor's own magnetic poles lock onto and follow this field, causing the rotor to turn at exactly synchronous speed (determined purely by supply frequency and pole count) regardless of load. A synchronous motor cannot start from standstill on its own, so typically needs an auxiliary starting method - a damper/amortisseur winding acting like a squirrel cage to start it as an induction motor before the DC field is applied, or a separate starting motor.

(b) Induction motor: the stator winding, energised from the three-phase supply, produces a rotating magnetic field. The rotor - typically a squirrel cage design (solid conducting bars short-circuited at each end by end rings, no external electrical connection) - has this rotating field sweep across it, inducing currents in the rotor bars purely by electromagnetic induction. These induced currents create their own magnetic field, which interacts with the stator's rotating field to produce torque, dragging the rotor around. The rotor must always turn slightly slower than the rotating field (slip), which sustains the induced current - an induction motor never reaches true synchronous speed under load, distinguishing it from the synchronous motor above.
answers.examiner_focus: August 2020's verified feedback for this occurrence is minimal - only a small number of candidates attempted it, mixed results. The core conceptual distinction is the more valuable point: a synchronous motor locks to exact synchronous speed via a separately-excited rotor and needs help starting; an induction motor never quite reaches synchronous speed (running with slip) but needs no separate excitation supply and starts on its own. Also verified December 2024.

answers.question_text: (a) Sketch a cross section through an a.c. induction motor. (5) (b) Describe the construction of the a.c induction motor sketched in part (a). (5)
answers.answer_text:
(a) Cross section showing the stator (outer laminated core with windings) surrounding the rotor, separated by a small air gap, mounted on a shaft supported by bearings in end shields bolted to the frame - either a side elevation (along the shaft axis) or a front/radial cross-section is acceptable.

(b) The stator consists of a laminated silicon-steel core - thin, insulated laminations reducing eddy current losses - housed in an outer cast iron or steel frame, with slots on its inner circumference holding the three-phase stator winding. The rotor (squirrel cage) sits inside, separated by the air gap, mounted on a shaft supported by bearings in end shields bolted to each end of the frame. Cooling is typically provided by a shaft-mounted fan drawing air through ventilation ducts in the frame and over the windings, with terminal boxes on the frame providing the connection point for supply cables.
answers.examiner_focus: March 2024: reasonably well answered, with credit given flexibly for either sketch orientation in part (a) - there's no single mandatory view. In part (b), some candidates described the motor's operation rather than its construction - the question asks specifically and only for construction. Also verified December 2025.
answers.sketch_description: Radial cross-section circle: outer ring labelled 'Stator core + windings', inner ring labelled 'Rotor (squirrel cage)', thin gap between them labelled 'Air gap', central circle labelled 'Shaft'. Alternative side-elevation option noted: shaft running horizontally through end shields/bearings into the frame.

answers.question_text: (a) Describe, with the aid of a sketch, the constructional details of a squirrel cage rotor as fitted in an induction motor. (7) (b) Explain why some rotors have a double cage. (3)
answers.answer_text:
(a) The rotor core is built up from thin, insulated laminated steel sheets stacked onto the rotor shaft. Running axially through slots around the circumference are solid conducting bars - typically copper or aluminium, in smaller motors often die-cast aluminium bars and end rings formed in a single casting operation with integral cooling fins. These bars are short-circuited together at each end by continuous conducting end rings, forming a closed conducting cage - hence 'squirrel cage.' There is no external electrical connection to the rotor at all - no slip rings, no brushes - since current is induced directly into the bars by the stator's rotating magnetic field, with the end rings providing the necessary circuit path.

(b) A double-cage rotor has two separate conductor bars per slot: an outer cage with higher resistance near the rotor surface, and an inner cage with lower resistance deeper in the core. At starting (high slip, high induced frequency), current flows predominantly through the outer high-resistance cage due to a skin/reactance effect, giving high starting torque. As the motor accelerates and slip falls, current transfers progressively to the inner low-resistance cage, giving good running efficiency at normal speed - both strong starting torque and efficient running performance, a compromise a simple single-cage design can't achieve as well.
answers.examiner_focus: Both verified sittings (March 2021, July 2023) show this question was reasonably well answered - a genuinely solid, well-understood topic without a specific recurring trap flagged in either report. Worth grounding the double-cage explanation in the actual skin-effect/reactance behaviour rather than a vague statement it 'improves starting' without explaining why. Also verified October 2024 (feedback: candidates unnecessarily sketched the stator when only the rotor was asked for, and described operation instead of construction - same construction-vs-operation trap as the cross-section question).
