Shaft running through the centre. Caption: 'No external electrical connection - closed conducting cage.'

answers.question_text: Describe how the starting torque of electric induction motors may be improved by using EACH of the following: (a) wound rotor; (5) (b) double cage. (5)
answers.answer_text:
(a) Wound rotor (slip-ring) motor: instead of a squirrel cage, the rotor carries its own three-phase winding, brought out via slip rings and brushes to external variable resistors. At starting, full external resistance is inserted in series with the rotor circuit - increasing rotor circuit resistance shifts the point of maximum torque toward higher slip, closer to standstill conditions, giving a high starting torque with a correspondingly lower starting current than an equivalent squirrel cage motor started direct-on-line. As the motor accelerates, this external resistance is progressively cut out in steps (via a rotor starter/controller), shifting maximum torque back toward normal running slip, until at zero added resistance the motor runs as a standard induction motor with rotor windings short-circuited via the slip rings.

(b) Double cage: as above - the outer, higher-resistance cage dominates at starting, giving strong starting torque, but achieved entirely passively through the rotor's own construction, with no external resistors, slip rings, or controller needed at all.
answers.examiner_focus: March 2022: part (a) was poorly answered, with the marker's own commentary noting wound rotor control is increasingly viewed as outdated technology, largely superseded by variable frequency drives - a reminder older technology can remain fully examinable even if less familiar. Part (b): some candidates got the two cages 'the wrong way round' - the outer, higher-resistance cage dominates at starting; the inner, lower-resistance cage dominates at running - easy to state backwards under exam pressure if not firmly fixed beforehand.

answers.question_text: With reference to three-phase induction motor starters: (a) explain why star-delta starters are employed; (2) (b) explain what is meant by reduced voltage starting in the context of star-delta starters; (2) (c) explain, with the aid of a power circuit, the sequence of operation of a star-delta starter. (6)
answers.answer_text:
(a) To reduce the very high starting current a large induction motor would otherwise draw if started direct-on-line (typically 5-7x full-load running current) - this large inrush causes excessive voltage dip on the ship's electrical system and unnecessary thermal/mechanical stress on the motor and supply cables.

(b) During the star starting phase, the motor's stator windings (normally connected in delta for running) are instead temporarily connected in star, applying roughly 58% (1/root-3) of normal line voltage across each winding. Since starting current is proportional to applied voltage, and the star connection itself further changes the current relationship, the combined effect reduces line starting current to roughly one-third of direct-on-line delta starting. Since torque is proportional to voltage squared, starting torque is also reduced to roughly one-third - meaning star-delta starting is only suitable for loads that don't need high starting torque, such as pumps or fans starting unloaded or lightly loaded.

(c) At starting, a star contactor connects the three stator winding ends together at a common star point, while a main/line contactor connects the winding starts to the three-phase supply - giving the reduced-voltage star connection. After a preset time delay, allowing the motor to accelerate to around 80-85% of full speed, the star contactor opens, and a delta contactor closes shortly after, reconnecting the same three windings in delta configuration directly across full line voltage. An electrical interlock between star and delta contactors ensures they can never close simultaneously, since that would create a direct short circuit across two winding ends.
answers.examiner_focus: Both verified sittings (October 2017, July 2019) show this question was well answered, with no specific recurring error flagged. The main value is making sure part (c) genuinely shows the sequence and the interlock, not just the two connection states in isolation.
answers.sketch_description: Three-phase supply at top feeding down through a 'Main contactor' box to the motor windings (circle). From the motor, one line to a 'Delta contactor' box (labelled 'closes after time delay'), one line to a 'Star contactor' box (labelled 'open for starting only, then opens').

answers.question_text: (a) State the consequences of using direct on line starters for comparatively large sized a.c. induction motors. (2) (b) Describe, with the aid of a sketch, an electronic soft starting system that may be used for large sized a.c. induction motors. (8)
answers.answer_text:
(a) A very high starting current (5-7x full-load running current) causes a significant voltage dip on the ship's electrical system, affecting other connected equipment. The sudden, uncontrolled application of near-full torque at starting also imposes high mechanical shock and stress on the motor shaft, coupling, and driven load.

(b) An electronic soft starter uses a back-to-back thyristor pair (or triac) in each of the three supply lines, controlling the RMS voltage applied to the motor by varying thyristor firing angle - the same phase-angle control principle as the AVR, applied to the motor's supply rather than a generator's field. At the start, the firing angle is set so only a small fraction of each half-cycle passes, giving a low initial voltage and correspondingly low starting current and torque. Over a set ramp-up period (typically several seconds), the firing angle is progressively advanced, smoothly increasing applied voltage, current and torque in a controlled ramp. Once close to full running speed, the thyristors are fully gated on; a bypass contactor then typically closes across the thyristors to carry running current directly, avoiding continuous heat dissipation in the thyristors and improving reliability. The same arrangement can provide a controlled ramp-down (soft stop), useful for loads like pumps where sudden stopping risks damaging pressure transients.
answers.examiner_focus: December 2019's feedback was simply positive - a good, well-answered question. October 2021's feedback flags something specific and important: a star-delta starter is NOT the same thing as an electronic soft starter - both are 'reduced voltage starting' methods broadly, but they work on entirely different principles (mechanical switching between two fixed states vs continuous thyristor-based voltage ramping). Also verified July 2025.
answers.sketch_description: Three-phase supply on the left feeding through a 'Thyristor pairs (one per phase, firing angle ramps)' box into a 'Motor' circle on the right. A 'Bypass' contactor box shown in a dashed line bridging around the thyristor box, labelled 'closes once at full speed'.

answers.question_text: Describe, with the aid of a circuit diagram, a synchro-converter for the variable speed control of a.c. motors. (10)
answers.answer_text: A synchro-converter provides variable speed control for AC motors by allowing the motor's supply frequency itself to be varied, since a motor's synchronous speed is directly proportional to supply frequency. The ship's fixed-frequency AC supply is first rectified to DC via a rectifier bridge - the same principle as the shaft generator frequency converter, but running in the opposite direction: fixed-frequency AC in, DC link, variable-frequency AC out. This DC link feeds an inverter, whose switching devices (thyristors or IGBTs) synthesise an AC output at whatever frequency - and corresponding voltage, maintaining a constant volts-per-hertz ratio to preserve motor flux and torque capability - is needed for the desired speed. Varying the inverter's switching frequency directly and smoothly varies the motor's running speed across a wide range, without needing to physically change the motor's pole configuration - unlike simpler methods such as pole-changing motors, which only offer a few fixed speed steps.
answers.examiner_focus: July 2024's feedback simply notes very few candidates attempted this question at all - worth treating as a strong candidate for deliberate revision precisely because so few currently have confident command of it.
answers.sketch_description: Block diagram: 'Fixed-frequency AC supply' box -> 'Rectifier' box -> 'DC link' box -> 'Inverter' box -> 'Variable-frequency AC output to motor' box. Caption: 'Inverter switching frequency sets motor speed.'

answers.question_text: With reference to overload protection for electric motors, describe the principle of operation of EACH of the following types of overload relay: (a) thermal; (3) (b) magnetic; (3) (c) electronic. (4)
answers.answer_text:
(a) Thermal overload relay: uses a bimetallic strip - two dissimilar metals bonded together with different thermal expansion rates - heated either directly by motor current or via a heater element carrying a scaled-down proportion of it. As current rises above rated value, the strip heats and bends due to differential expansion; once bent sufficiently, it operates a trip mechanism, opening the contactor coil circuit. This gives an inherently time-delayed response roughly mimicking the motor's own thermal heating behaviour.

(b) Magnetic overload relay: uses a solenoid coil carrying motor current (directly or via a CT), whose magnetic pull on a plunger increases with current. Above a preset threshold, the magnetic force pulls the plunger through its full travel, operating a trip contact - often combined with a dashpot to give a time-current characteristic rather than a purely instantaneous trip.

(c) Electronic overload relay: uses current transformers to sense actual motor current, feeding a microprocessor-based circuit that calculates a thermal model of the motor's heating from sensed current, elapsed time, and a pre-programmed thermal time constant - tripping when this calculated model indicates the motor has reached its thermal limit. Offers more precise, adjustable settings and additional protection functions (phase loss, phase imbalance, stall, ground fault) built into one unit.
answers.examiner_focus: October 2022's feedback is exceptionally direct: this was the most poorly answered question in the entire paper. One sharp point: 'a fuse is not a thermal relay' - candidates apparently substituted a fuse as their answer for the thermal type. For magnetic and electronic types, most candidates had genuinely no idea, guessing or leaving it blank. The marker explicitly states this exact question will likely reappear. Also verified March 2025 and March 2026.

answers.question_text: With reference to a.c.induction motors: (a) state, with reasons, the type of fuses used for protection; (2) (b) explain the effects of single phasing; (3) (c) describe how thermistors can be used to protect the motor; (3) (d) state TWO types of relay that provide electrical overload protection. (2)
answers.answer_text:
(a) HRC (High Rupturing Capacity) fuses, chosen for their ability to safely interrupt high fault currents without violent rupture, with well-defined characteristics suited to motor circuit protection.

(b) If a running motor loses one of its three supply phases, it continues running on the remaining two phases but shows clear symptoms: increased noise, increased vibration, and a noticeable reduction in speed, since available torque drops significantly on two phases. If the motor is stopped in this condition, it will not be able to restart, since starting torque on two phases from standstill is generally insufficient.

(c) Thermistors (typically PTC type) are solid-state temperature sensors embedded directly within the motor's stator windings, at the point of expected maximum heating. As winding temperature rises, the thermistor's electrical resistance changes sharply once a threshold temperature is reached; a monitoring relay circuit detects this resistance change and trips the motor's contactor before winding insulation is damaged. Because it sits directly in the windings, it responds to actual winding temperature from any cause, not just current overload.

(d) Thermal (bimetallic) relay and magnetic (or electronic) relay.
answers.examiner_focus: December 2021: three distinct genuine points. Many candidates missed the specific expected answer (HRC fuse) in part (a). Part (b) asks for the SYMPTOMS of single phasing (noise, vibration, slowing, failure to restart), not the CONSEQUENCES of ignoring it (motor burnout) - several candidates answered the wrong framing. Part (c): thermistors do NOT 'expand' under heat - that's how a bimetallic strip works; a thermistor's resistance changes with temperature. Several candidates also didn't know thermistors sit embedded directly inside the motor windings, not in an external control panel.

answers.question_text: With reference to insulated and earthed electrical systems operating at High Voltage: (a) state the regulations pertaining to tankers; (4) (b) describe, with the aid of a sketch, a method to detect earth leakage in EACH of the following systems: (i) earthed; (3) (ii) insulated. (3)
answers.answer_text:
(a) On tankers, HV electrical equipment located in or near hazardous cargo/pump room zones must be of an appropriately certified explosion-protected type - intrinsically safe, flameproof, increased safety, or pressurised - since HV arcing presents a significantly elevated ignition risk in a potentially explosive atmosphere. HV switchgear and cabling must be routed and segregated away from hazardous zones wherever practicable, and where HV equipment must be sited in or near such areas, additional measures (physical segregation, gas-detection interlocks, positive pressurisation of enclosures) are specifically required.

(b)(i) Earthed system: since the neutral is earthed via an NER, a genuine current flows to earth during a fault. Detection uses a current transformer around the neutral-to-earth connection (or a core-balance CT arrangement), feeding a relay that operates once current above a preset threshold is detected.

(b)(ii) Insulated system: since there's no deliberate earth connection, only a small capacitive leakage current results. Detection uses the instrument-type method - equal high-value resistors from each phase to a common point, feeding a sensitive milliammeter - scaled and insulated appropriately for the higher HV voltage level.
answers.examiner_focus: No specific marker feedback located for this July 2016 occurrence.

answers.question_text: With reference to testing High Voltage equipment: (a) explain why earthing down is considered essential; (2) (b) state the operating voltage for an insulation resistance tester (meggar) suitable for 6.6 KV equipment; (1) (c) describe how an insulation resistance test is carried out on High Voltage equipment, making reference to personnel safety; (5) (d) explain why infra red temperature measurement is used on High Voltage equipment. (2)
answers.answer_text:
(a) 'Earthing down' means physically connecting HV conductors and equipment to earth via a dedicated earthing device or switch before personnel work on or test it. Even after isolating the supply and proving dead, HV equipment can retain a dangerous stored charge from its own capacitance, or could become accidentally re-energised from an unexpected back-feed. Earthing down provides a continuously visible, physically connected discharge path, guaranteeing the equipment cannot become live while work is in progress.

(b) A considerably higher test voltage than standard LV 500V - commonly around 5,000V DC for equipment of this class.

(c) Obtain a permit to work and isolate the equipment at every possible supply point, locking off each one. Prove dead using an approved high-voltage live-line tester rated specifically for the voltage involved. Apply temporary earthing-down connections to discharge any stored capacitive charge before work begins. Remove these earths specifically and only for the duration of the actual IR test itself, following a carefully controlled sequence. Connect the HV insulation tester and apply the appropriate test voltage, taking readings as required. On completion, safely discharge the equipment - typically using a discharge rod or earthing stick - then re-apply earthing-down connections until work is fully complete. Throughout, appropriate HV-rated PPE should be worn, with a second person present.

(d) It allows checking for abnormal heating - a developing loose connection, an overloaded joint, degrading insulation - entirely without touching or approaching the live HV equipment directly.
answers.examiner_focus: July 2023's report is exceptionally direct, flagging genuine errors across all four parts. Part (a): candidates confused 'earthing down' with ongoing insulation monitoring - a completely different, continuous operational concept. Part (b): despite the question explicitly stating 6.6kV, many candidates still answered with a low-voltage test figure (1,000V or less). Part (c) - most critically - very few candidates mentioned proving dead with an approved live-line tester at all, a fundamentally life-critical HV safety step whose near-universal omission is a serious, explicitly documented gap.
answers.sketch_description: Flowchart: 'Isolate, lock off' box -> 'Prove dead, HV live-line tester' box -> 'Earth down, discharge charge' box -> 'Remove earths for test only' box -> 'IR test, apply' box. Caption below: 'After test: discharge with earthing stick, then re-earth down until work is complete.'

answers.question_text: With reference to the protection of High Voltage electric a.c. motors: (a) state the type of fuses that are fitted and how they prevent single phasing; (3) (b) describe the operation of EACH of the following direct temperature sensors: (i) resistance temperature device; (3) (ii) thermistor. (4)
answers.answer_text:
(a) HV motors typically use HRC fuses combined with a striker-pin (tripping pin) mechanism. When any one fuse operates, its striker pin mechanically ejects and operates a trip linkage on the associated contactor or breaker - disconnecting all three phases together, not just the phase whose fuse blew. An ordinary HRC fuse alone only protects and interrupts its own single phase - the striker-pin-to-trip-linkage arrangement, tying all three phases' disconnection together, is what genuinely prevents single phasing.

(b)(i) RTD: a precision resistance element (typically platinum, Pt100) whose resistance increases in a precisely known relationship with temperature. Embedded in the winding, a monitoring circuit continuously measures this resistance and converts it to an accurate, continuously-variable temperature reading, able to drive both an alarm and a trip at different thresholds.

(b)(ii) Thermistor: a semiconductor sensor embedded in the winding whose resistance changes sharply once a threshold temperature is reached, giving a simpler go/no-go protection signal rather than a continuously variable reading.
answers.examiner_focus: March 2023's feedback is genuinely specific and valuable. The crux of part (a): 'preventing single phasing' specifically requires disconnecting all three phases together - the most common wrong answer was simply 'HRC fuse' without the striker-pin/trip-linkage detail. Part (b): the marker notes both RTDs and thermistors have appeared as standalone topics before, yet many candidates still didn't know what a thermistor actually is or how it protects windings - the same gap documented for the general induction-motor question. Also verified July 2026 (candidate's own sitting).

answers.question_text: (a) Explain the term power factor. (2) (b) Explain why it is detrimental to have a low power factor. (2) (c) Explain, with the aid of phasor diagrams, how a synchronous motor may be used to assist in power factor correction. (6)
answers.answer_text:
(a) The ratio of real power (kW, doing useful work) to apparent power (kVA, the total the supply system must actually deliver) - mathematically, PF = cos(phi), where phi is the phase angle between voltage and current. Unity power factor means all delivered power is useful; a power factor below 1 means part of the supplied current is reactive, sustaining magnetic fields in inductive loads like motors and transformers, and this reactive current still has to be generated and carried even though it performs no useful work.

(b) For a given real (kW) demand, a lower power factor means a higher apparent power - and therefore higher current - must flow through generators, cables, and switchgear to deliver that same useful power. Generators must be oversized in kVA relative to useful kW; cables and switchgear must carry the higher current, requiring larger conductors and increasing I-squared-R losses; voltage regulation is generally poorer, since more of the source's capacity is consumed by reactive current.

(c) A synchronous motor's field excitation can be deliberately over-excited beyond what's needed to maintain synchronism. When over-excited, the motor draws a leading current from the supply, rather than the lagging current a normal induction motor draws - effectively behaving as a source of leading reactive power. In a phasor diagram, a typical lagging load's current phasor sits at angle phi behind the voltage phasor, with a large reactive component. Adding an over-excited synchronous motor's leading current phasor to the system partially cancels that lagging reactive component when summed vectorially - the resulting overall system current phasor ends up at a smaller angle relative to voltage, meaning an improved, closer-to-unity system power factor.
answers.examiner_focus: October 2022's feedback for this question was simply 'no problems' - straightforward and positive. Also verified March 2024 and October 2025.
answers.sketch_description: Phasor diagram: horizontal reference arrow labelled 'V (voltage reference)'. A lagging current phasor drawn above/behind it at an angle, labelled 'I load (lagging)'. A leading current phasor drawn on the other side, labelled 'I synchronous motor (leading)'. A resultant phasor (vector sum of the two) drawn with a visibly smaller angle to the voltage reference than the original lagging load phasor, labelled 'I resultant (improved PF)'.

answers.question_text: (a) Explain the meaning of EACH of the following types of electrical safety equipment: (i) intrinsically safe; (2) (ii) flameproof; (2) (iii) increased safety. (2) (b) State the electrical tests for equipment in hazardous areas, describing the safety precautions. (4)
answers.answer_text:
(a)(i) Intrinsically safe: equipment designed so the electrical energy available in the circuit is deliberately limited - via current-limiting resistors, safety barriers, and low-voltage/low-power design - to a level too low to ever produce an ignition-capable spark or sufficient heating, even under fault conditions.

(a)(ii) Flameproof (Exd): equipment in a robust enclosure designed so that if an internal explosion occurs, the enclosure contains it and cools the escaping gases sufficiently, through carefully machined flame-path joints, that the surrounding explosive atmosphere isn't ignited.

(a)(iii) Increased safety (Exe): equipment built with extra design margins specifically to eliminate the possibility of sparks, arcs, or excessive surface temperatures arising in normal operation - generous margins in insulation, clearances, and creepage distances, typically with no normally-arcing components inside.

(b) Insulation resistance testing and continuity testing of earth bonding are typically carried out, but not with the equipment live in the hazardous area unless the space is confirmed gas-free and covered by an electrical work permit specific to that area. A gas detector must confirm the atmosphere is free of explosive concentration before any spark-capable testing, and for flameproof equipment specifically, enclosures must be inspected for damage to the machined flame-path joints.
answers.examiner_focus: This exact question has recurred many times - the marker notes it appeared most recently in December 2019 (October 2017 sitting), yet performance remained poor in March 2023. Part (a) needs a genuine explanation of what makes each type actually safe, not a bare name or short phrase - most candidates scored only half marks here. Part (b) shows a real, specific weak spot: candidates gave generic buzzwords like 'risk assessment' and 'wear correct PPE' without ever specifying what testing should happen or what the precautions concretely are.

answers.question_text: (a) Explain the meaning of EACH of the following types of electrical equipment: (i) intrinsically safe; (2) (ii) flameproof; (2) (iii) increased safety; (2) (iv) pressurised enclosure. (2) (b) State TWO types of lighting equipment that may be installed in the pump room areas of a crude petroleum carrier. (2)
answers.answer_text:
(a)(i)-(iii): as in the electrical-tests variant above.

(a)(iv) Pressurised enclosure (Exp): equipment housed in an enclosure continuously purged and maintained at a pressure slightly above the surrounding atmosphere, using clean air or inert gas, specifically to prevent surrounding explosive gas from entering at all. Since the positive internal pressure reliably excludes the external atmosphere, normally-arcing components (switchgear, contactors) can safely be housed inside - typically fitted with a pressure-loss alarm/trip to de-energise the equipment if the purge is lost.

(b) Bulkhead-mounted fittings viewed through a fixed, sealed glass port from an adjacent non-hazardous space - the light fitting itself sits entirely outside the hazardous pump room, shining through a gas-tight window. Alternatively, flameproof (Exd) or intrinsically safe fittings specifically certified for direct installation within the hazardous pump room itself, used where bulkhead-through-glass lighting can't achieve the coverage needed.
answers.examiner_focus: No specific feedback located for the July 2016 occurrence. December 2019 reports this as 'reasonably well answered' - generally positive, with no specific pitfall flagged for that sitting.

answers.question_text: With reference to lithium-ion batteries: (a) explain why this type of battery has been adopted for shipboard use; (4) (b) state ONE advantage and ONE disadvantage of lithium-ion batteries; (2) (c) define EACH of the following terms: (i) cell drift; (2) (ii) thermal runaway. (2)
answers.answer_text:
(a) Lithium-ion batteries offer significantly higher energy density than lead-acid or nickel-cadmium batteries - more stored energy per unit weight/volume - which matters directly for battery-hybrid and fully electric propulsion where weight and space are at a premium. They support much faster charge/discharge rates and more charge cycles before degrading, and their use in hybrid propulsion directly supports improved fuel efficiency and reduced emissions, since batteries can be used to load-level engine operation and enable periods of battery-only operation.

(b) Advantage: significantly higher energy density than lead-acid. Disadvantage: genuine risk of thermal runaway if damaged, overcharged, or internally faulted, requiring more sophisticated battery management and fire-suppression arrangements.

(c)(i) Cell drift: in a series-connected battery pack, individual cells can gradually diverge in state of charge or internal characteristics over repeated cycles, even though the whole pack is charged/discharged together - requiring active cell-balancing as part of the battery management system.

(c)(ii) Thermal runaway: a self-sustaining, escalating chemical reaction within a cell - triggered by internal short-circuit, physical damage, overcharging, or excessive heat - where the cell's own internal heating accelerates the reaction further, in an uncontrolled positive-feedback cycle, potentially proceeding to cell rupture, fire, and propagation to adjacent cells.
answers.examiner_focus: March 2022's report states plainly that all the answers to this question are found in MGN 550, yet many candidates had little idea how to answer it, particularly missing fuel efficiency and emissions reduction in part (a). July 2025 gives an even richer expansion: the examiner states this question is NOT about lithium-ion versus alkaline/acid chemistry, but about overall fuel efficiency, reduced emissions, noise, vibration, hybrid power systems, and reduced maintenance costs - with the fuller answer found in the relevant M Notice (MGN 550).

answers.question_text: (a) With reference to an alkaline battery cell: (i) describe a typical cell, stating the materials used; (4) (ii) describe the process that takes place during discharge and charge; (2) (iii) state the effects of overcharge. (2) (b) State the advantages of an alkaline cell compared with a lead acid cell. (2)
answers.answer_text:
(a)(i) A nickel-cadmium alkaline cell typically uses a positive electrode of nickel hydroxide/nickel oxyhydroxide, a negative electrode of cadmium, and an electrolyte of potassium hydroxide solution - an alkaline electrolyte, distinguishing this cell type from the sulphuric acid electrolyte of a lead-acid battery.

(a)(ii) During discharge, cadmium at the negative plate oxidises while nickel oxyhydroxide at the positive plate is reduced, both reactions consuming/producing hydroxide ions that remain within the electrolyte rather than changing its concentration significantly. On charge, an externally applied current drives these reactions in reverse.

(a)(iii) Sustained overcharge causes excess energy to be dissipated as gassing - decomposition of water in the electrolyte into hydrogen and oxygen gas - requiring adequate ventilation, and can lead to increased water loss requiring periodic topping up.

(b) Alkaline cells are considerably more tolerant of overcharge and deep discharge without permanent damage, have a longer overall service life, and can survive extended periods in a discharged state without the sulphation damage that would ruin a lead-acid cell - well suited to emergency/standby applications where a battery may sit unused for long periods.
answers.examiner_focus: Verified October 2018. Genuine marker feedback found near this diet's report mentioned MGN 550 and 'a new question' but reads as though it more likely belongs to the lithium-ion topic rather than this long-established alkaline cell question - not confident enough in that pairing to cite it here.

answers.question_text: (a) With reference to battery systems for emergency purposes, explain the precautions that must be taken with regard to personnel safety, storage and maintenance. (7) (b) Explain how batteries are kept at the correct rate of charge. (3)
answers.answer_text:
(a) Personnel safety: appropriate PPE (acid/alkali-resistant gloves, eye protection), and awareness that batteries produce explosive hydrogen gas during charging - no naked flames, smoking, or spark-producing activity near batteries, particularly during and just after charging.

Storage: batteries must be kept in a dedicated, well-ventilated space specifically to disperse hydrogen gas before it can accumulate to an explosive concentration; lighting fixtures within the space must themselves be explosion-proof/non-sparking; batteries must be securely mounted or racked to prevent movement or toppling in a seaway.

Maintenance: regular checks of electrolyte level (topping up with distilled water where required), inspecting for terminal corrosion, periodic specific gravity or voltage checks to confirm state of charge and condition, confirming security of mounting and wiring.

(b) Batteries are typically maintained on continuous 'float' charge from a dedicated charger, supplying a small trickle current sufficient to offset natural self-discharge without overcharging. The charger's output is voltage-regulated, similar in principle to an AVR, adjusting automatically as needed, with a periodic higher-rate 'equalising' or 'boost' charge sometimes applied to correct any imbalance between individual cells.
answers.examiner_focus: October 2017's genuinely specific feedback: the STORAGE aspect of this question was consistently neglected - candidates focused on personnel safety and maintenance while forgetting the physical storage environment itself, specifically ventilation and lighting requirements and how batteries are physically secured. Worth deliberately writing a distinct storage-focused section rather than folding it into general safety commentary. Also verified July 2021 and March 2022. Reported (unverified) at December 2025 with divergent 'also asked in' tags (Dec 2022, Mar 2018) not independently confirmed against the official papers - flagged as an open discrepancy rather than resolved.

answers.question_text: With reference to large electrical transformers on board ships: (a) state where these transformers may be used; (1) (b) state a typical efficiency range for a transformer; (1) (c) state the regulations pertaining to transformers; (3) (d) state the protective devices that are fitted; (2) (e) describe the maintenance requirements. (3)
answers.answer_text:
(a) Stepping down high-voltage generation/distribution (e.g. 6.6kV or 11kV) to 440V for general ship's services, or supplying HV equipment (large bow thrusters, HV motors) directly, or for shore power connection.

(b) Very high, typically in the region of 97-99%, since large power transformers are among the most efficient electrical machines, with losses limited mainly to core (iron) and winding (copper) losses.

(c) Construction and testing to recognised standards, adequate cooling rated for the intended environment, and - specifically for continuity-of-supply reasons - requirements ensuring the transformer arrangement doesn't create a single point of failure for essential services, plus specific segregation, access, and warning requirements where HV is involved.

(d) Overcurrent/short-circuit protection on both primary and secondary sides, winding temperature monitoring with alarm and trip stages, a Buchholz relay on oil-filled types (detecting gas evolution from an internal fault), and differential protection on larger units.

(e) Regular insulation resistance testing, inspection and maintenance of cooling systems (fans, oil condition and level, radiators), visual checks for oil leaks/corrosion/loose connections, periodic testing of protective devices and alarms, and for oil-filled types, oil sampling and dissolved gas analysis to detect a developing internal fault.
answers.examiner_focus: One of the most consistently and clearly documented recurring errors in the entire dataset - flagged explicitly across two of three verified sittings (March 2021, October 2023). Candidates repeatedly conflate part (c) 'regulations' with part (d) 'protective devices,' repeating the same content across both. October 2023's report adds a specific clarifying note: part (c) is more about continuity of supply considerations, not a restatement of the protective device list. Also verified October 2017.

answers.question_text: Describe the principle of operation of a ship's Impressed Current Cathodic Protection system. (Note: exact original question wording did not extract cleanly from the source PDF for this instance - genuine marker feedback confirms this topic was tested and confused with Marine Growth Prevention Systems, tied to an October 2019 sitting.)
answers.answer_text:
An ICCP system protects the ship's underwater steel hull from electrochemical corrosion by making the hull the cathode of a deliberately imposed electrical circuit, rather than relying on sacrificial metal being consumed. Permanently fitted anodes (typically platinised titanium or similar inert, non-consumable material) are mounted on the underwater hull, connected to a DC power supply via a control unit. A reference electrode, also mounted on the hull, continuously monitors the hull's actual electrical potential relative to seawater. The control unit compares this measured potential against a target protective potential and automatically adjusts the DC current fed to the anodes to maintain the hull at the correct protective level.

Unlike a sacrificial anode system (where zinc or aluminium anodes are consumed over time and require periodic physical replacement), ICCP anodes are essentially inert and don't consume themselves - protection current is generated electronically and adjusted continuously, giving more precise, controllable, longer-lasting protection without needing regular anode replacement in drydock.
answers.examiner_focus: October 2019's genuine marker's report: 'Few candidates answered this question and very few described an ICCP system. Most misinterpreted the question as a Marine Growth Prevention System and described copper and aluminium anodes in a sea chest.' ICCP protects the external hull from corrosion; MGPS releases trace metal ions inside seawater cooling systems to discourage marine growth - completely different purposes despite both involving anodes. A separate March 2024 General-paper sitting corroborates the same confusion pattern from the reverse direction (an MGPS question answered as if it were ICCP).

answers.question_text: State the main electrical items covered in a Classification Society periodical survey. (10)
answers.answer_text: Insulation resistance testing of generators, motors, and distribution circuits; condition and function testing of all main and emergency switchboard protective devices including overcurrent, short circuit, reverse power, and preferential tripping relays; testing of the emergency generator's automatic starting and changeover arrangement, confirming it starts and connects within the required time; inspection and testing of the emergency battery system, including capacity and condition; visual inspection of cabling, particularly in hazardous areas, checking cable transits and gland integrity; functional testing of earth fault/insulation monitoring devices; inspection of large transformers, including oil condition where applicable and protective device operation; testing of steering gear electrical control and alarm systems; and confirmation that documentation - test certificates, wiring diagrams, and previous survey/repair records - is current and consistent with the vessel's actual installed equipment.
